mascot.pet.guide.board.hello: This is the board~ Hot, Today and Weekly are in the row up top.
mascot.pet.guide.board.q1: What's the difference between Today and Hot?
mascot.pet.guide.board.a1: Today only counts cards listed in the last 24 hours, while Hot ranks every card on the site, and both put the highest heat first.
mascot.pet.guide.board.q2: How do I see just one genre?
mascot.pet.guide.board.a2: Just tap a genre tag. You can pick several. Genres you don't want to see can be hidden in settings.
mascot.pet.guide.board.q3: Can I jump to a card if I know its number?
mascot.pet.guide.board.a3: Yep! Type the card number in the search box and press Enter to jump right to it.
mascot.pet.guide.board.a4: Heat comes from the credits other players spend on a card~ Longer chats and more players push it higher, and the author's own play doesn't count.
mascot.pet.guide.search.hello: What are you looking for? You can search character names, source titles and tags~
mascot.pet.guide.search.a1: Try the source title or a tag instead. Source titles work in Traditional or Simplified Chinese, and short names work too.
mascot.pet.guide.search.q2: Can I see just one source?
mascot.pet.guide.search.a2: Yep, there's a source filter above the results.
mascot.pet.guide.editor.hello: Writing a card? Tap me if anything's unclear~
mascot.pet.guide.editor.q1: What do I have to fill in?
mascot.pet.guide.editor.a1: Three things: name, persona and opening message. Any section on the left with a red dot is still missing something.
mascot.pet.guide.editor.q2: How do I get on the board?
mascot.pet.guide.editor.a2: Hit Publish, answer the rating questions and confirm the source, and it goes to review. Once it passes, it's on the board. There's a weekly listing quota.
mascot.pet.guide.editor.a3: Yep, the test chat panel on the side lets you chat with your card right away.
mascot.pet.guide.card.hello: This is the card page. Hit "Start chat" to play~
mascot.pet.guide.card.a1: It goes into your Library so you can find it in one tap. The author also gets to know someone likes it.
mascot.pet.guide.card.a2: They're everyone's ratings. A card with only a few votes won't shoot to the top from a single one.
mascot.pet.guide.card.a3: If the author has tips turned on, there's a tip button on this page. Comments and favorites count as support too!
mascot.pet.guide.author.hello: This is the author's page. Follow them and you'll get notified about new cards.
mascot.pet.guide.author.a1: When they post or update a card, the bell lets you know. You'll get it through push notifications or Discord DMs too if you've turned those on.
mascot.pet.guide.library.hello: Everything you've chatted with, favorited and followed is here.
mascot.pet.guide.library.a1: Chats save automatically. Hit "Continue chat" here to pick up where you left off.
mascot.pet.guide.library.q2: What's the difference between favorites and follows?
mascot.pet.guide.library.a2: You favorite cards and follow authors.
mascot.pet.guide.mine.hello: All your cards are here, and you can check their review status too.
mascot.pet.guide.mine.q1: How many cards can I list each week?
mascot.pet.guide.mine.a1: This week's listing quota is shown up top and resets every Monday. If you run out, you can use extra listing packs.
mascot.pet.guide.mine.q2: What if my card got rejected?
mascot.pet.guide.mine.a2: The reason is written on the card. Fix it up and submit again.
mascot.pet.guide.mine.q3: Editing a card that's already listed?
mascot.pet.guide.mine.a3: If you change the name, summary, cover, tags or opening message, it goes back to review.
mascot.pet.guide.wallet.hello: These are your credits. Chatting uses them.
mascot.pet.guide.wallet.a1: Credits with an expiry date. Once they expire, they're gone. You can see every entry in the history below.
mascot.pet.guide.wallet.a2: Hit Top up and you'll pay in the HarperHarbor console. Come back after paying and the credits will be there.
mascot.pet.guide.referral.hello: Invite your friends and you'll both get credits.
mascot.pet.guide.referral.a1: Send your friend your invite code or link. It counts once they sign up and enter it.
mascot.pet.guide.referral.q2: A friend gave me an invite code?
mascot.pet.guide.referral.a2: Enter it under "Enter invite code". There's a time limit, so do it within a few days of signing up.
mascot.pet.guide.badges.a1: Each badge shows its requirements and your progress. Playing cards, writing cards, favoriting and commenting all count.
mascot.pet.guide.badges.q2: Can I show off just a few?
mascot.pet.guide.badges.a2: You can pick a few as featured, or make the whole wall private.
mascot.pet.guide.community.hello: Link your Discord and I'll recognize you over there too!
mascot.pet.guide.community.a1: Chatting on Discord earns you XP and levels. I can also DM you notifications.
mascot.pet.guide.community.q2: How do I report a problem?
mascot.pet.guide.community.a2: You can open a report here, and support will follow up with you on Discord.
mascot.pet.guide.notifications.hello: Who replied to you and what your followed authors posted, it's all here.
mascot.pet.guide.notifications.q1: Want alerts even when you're off the site?
mascot.pet.guide.notifications.a1: Turn on browser push notifications, or link Discord so I can DM you.
mascot.pet.guide.notifications.a2: You can turn off on-site notifications or like notifications up top.
mascot.pet.guide.me.hello: This is your profile page. Your info and all kinds of shortcuts are here.
mascot.pet.guide.me.q1: How do I change my nickname and avatar?
mascot.pet.guide.me.a1: Just edit your profile on this page.
mascot.pet.guide.settings.hello: Set up your player persona here, plus what kind of content you want to see.
mascot.pet.guide.settings.a1: It decides what the characters in a card call you and who they think you are.
mascot.pet.guide.settings.q2: Don't want to see some genres?
mascot.pet.guide.settings.a2: Check them and they'll be hidden from the board and search. You can undo it anytime.
mascot.pet.guide.resources.hello: This is your asset library. Put any images for your cards here.
mascot.pet.guide.resources.q1: Anything to watch out for when renaming files?
mascot.pet.guide.resources.a1: Renaming a file or moving it to another folder changes its link, so update any cards that use it!
mascot.pet.guide.guide.hello: The card-writing guide~ It covers writing with an AI assistant and with the web editor.
mascot.pet.guide.guide.a1: An AI assistant is fastest. Just describe the character you want clearly. If you'd rather fine-tune it yourself, use the web editor.
mascot.pet.guide.developers.hello: Developer docs. Check here if you want to integrate or manage cards with code.
mascot.pet.guide.developers.a1: There's a command-line tool. Once an AI assistant sets it up, it can write and upload cards for you.
mascot.pet.guide.updates.hello: Everything that's changed on the site lately is here~
mascot.pet.guide.download.hello: Want {site} on your phone? Look here.
mascot.pet.guide.download.q1: How do I install it on iPhone?
mascot.pet.guide.download.a1: Open the site in Safari, tap Share, then choose "Add to Home Screen".
mascot.pet.guide.review.q1: What if I claim a card and don't get to it?
mascot.pet.guide.review.a1: If you don't act on it for a while after claiming, it goes back to the queue for someone else.
mascot.pet.guide.review.a2: Put it back in the queue and let another reviewer take a look. No need to force a call.

editor.world.lede: World mode: this card is a world with several characters. The world itself is the character definition under Persona, and the world-level lore is the Lorebook bound to this card; only the characters live here. Each turn the world first decides what happened and who is present, then up to a few characters answer in their own voice, each knowing only what they saw or were told.
editor.world.experimental: World mode is still experimental and may not behave as expected, so use it for testing and trying things out, and keep it off cards you plan to publish.
editor.world.disable: Turn world mode off (characters are removed when you save)
editor.world.maxSpeakers: Characters who may speak per turn
editor.world.strictness: How far the world honours what the player declares
editor.world.strictness.lenient: Lenient: what the player says happens
editor.world.strictness.balanced: Balanced: ordinary outcomes as stated; anything involving others or hidden facts is decided by the world
editor.world.strictness.strict: Strict: the player only states intent; the world decides every outcome
editor.world.char.name: Name
editor.world.char.id.hint: Lowercase letters, digits, underscore or hyphen; leave empty to derive it from the name. Do not change it after saving: past messages and pending events refer to it.
editor.world.char.profile.hint: One or two sentences the world and the other characters all know.
editor.world.char.description: Full definition (seen only by this character)
editor.world.char.description.hint: Can be long. It enters only this character's own context; the world and the other characters never see it.
editor.world.char.lorebook.hint: Same as the card's Lorebook: create one, import a file, or pick one you already have. It is recalled only when this character speaks; the other characters and the world never see it.
editor.state.lede: Card variables let the AI keep values such as affection, inventory and quests from turn to turn and update them as the story moves; the chat page can show them in a panel.
editor.state.data.error: The JSON has a format error. Check brackets, quotes and commas.
editor.state.data.errorAt: The JSON has a format error near line {line}. Check brackets, quotes and commas.
editor.state.data.notObject: The outermost level of the skeleton must be an object wrapped in curly braces.
editor.state.size: About {n} more characters sent each turn
editor.state.size.warn: About {n} more characters sent each turn. More values make every turn slower and more expensive.
editor.state.example.replace: The current skeleton is not valid JSON. Replace the whole skeleton with the example?
editor.state.rules.hint: For the AI: which value changes in which situation, and how. Sent with the values every turn.
editor.state.template.hint: HTML and CSS written in Handlebars. The chat page uses it to draw the current values as a panel; leave it empty for no panel.
editor.state.reject.convention: The variable format must be either value with a rule or values only.
editor.state.reject.data: The variable skeleton must be a valid JSON object. Fix it and save again.
editor.state.reject.data_size: The variable skeleton is over {dataKB} KB. Remove values you don't need and save again.
editor.state.reject.depth: The variable skeleton can be at most {depth} levels deep. Flatten the deepest parts and save again.
editor.state.reject.keys: The variable skeleton can hold at most {keys} items. Remove the ones you don't need and save again.
editor.state.reject.string_size: A text value in the variable skeleton is over {stringKB} KB. Shorten it and save again.
editor.state.reject.rules_text_size: Variable rules are over {rulesKB} KB. Shorten them and save again.
editor.state.reject.rule_paths_size: The rules attached to values add up to more than {pathsKB} KB. Shorten them and save again.
editor.state.reject.rule_path: A rule does not match any value in the skeleton. Check which value it is attached to.
editor.state.reject.template_size: The panel skin is over {templateKB} KB. Shorten it and save again.

editor.language.scriptHint: Players whose interface uses the same script see your text as written, and the rest see it converted, so pick the script the card is actually written in.
editor.detail.hint: The heart of the card: who they are, how they speak, what situation they're in. The more concrete, the more consistent the replies.
editor.contract.hint: What a reply should look like: how many paragraphs, whether to narrate, how to mark actions. Leave empty for the default.
editor.jailbreak.hint: Appended to every turn. Put the one or two rules that get forgotten most.
editor.welcome.hint: The first thing a player reads. Set the scene and the relationship here, or the story never starts.
editor.alternates.hint: A different way in, same story. Before the first message, players can swipe between them and pick one; the main opening is the default.
editor.openingPage.hint: This page appears at the top of every new chat and supports HTML, styles, and scripts; leave it empty to show only the choices.
editor.talkExample.hint: A few exchanges showing how this character talks. Two or three is plenty; more locks them in.
editor.background.hint: Portrait, 9:16. Also used as the chat background, avatar, and exported image. Keep important details inside the dashed safe zone.
editor.backgroundLandscape.hint: Used on wide screens, 16:9. If empty, the portrait cover is cropped instead.

This cookie has a fixed expiry of up to 13 months from when it is set; returning to the site does not extend it. Google Analytics also sets cookies on the site domain you are visiting to store the same visitor code.
privacy.analytics.p3: Google receives the visitor code, the types of pages viewed, and records of activity such as signing in, chatting, sharing and paying. When you go from this site to HarperHarbor to check out, the visitor code is also passed to the checkout site so we can connect a visit with a payment.
privacy.analytics.p4: After you sign in, we send Google a separate code generated for your account to link activity for that account across devices and the payment site. This code cannot be reversed to recover your original account number and is not your email address.
privacy.analytics.p5: When a payment is completed, we send Google the amount, currency and purchase category (a top-up or 30-Day Pass), and indicate whether the account has ever made a top-up or bought a 30-Day Pass. We also send records of related refunds.
privacy.analytics.p6: We do not send Google Analytics your conversation content, card names, author names, card numbers, original account number or email address.
privacy.analytics.p7: If your browser has Global Privacy Control (GPC) enabled, we do not set the visitor cookies described above or send analytics data to Google Analytics.

editor.reply.hint.agency.coauthor: The AI can also write what the player’s character says, thinks, does and decides, based on the character setup and current scene.
editor.reply.hint.agency.protect: The AI writes other characters and the world; what the player’s character says, thinks, does and decides is left to the player.
editor.reply.hint.length.auto: Automatic length lets the AI decide how long each reply runs, and the card’s own length rule still comes first.
editor.reply.hint.length.balanced: Replies land within about 30% of the target, and status panels are not counted.
editor.reply.hint.length.brief: Replies stay close to the target, which suits fast dialogue.
editor.reply.hint.length.detailed: Replies land within about 30% of the target, and with “Don’t write for me” on, longer targets tend to fill short turns with padding, so Automatic fits those better.
editor.reply.hint.length.long: Most models stop early at this length, so use Continue when a reply falls short.
editor.reply.hint.length.recommended: Recommended length aims for about 2 to 5 paragraphs and roughly 1500 words, which can turn into filler when “Don’t write for me” is on and your message is short, so Automatic fits those turns better.
editor.reply.hint.pace.advance: Moves other characters and events forward, adding new developments when they fit.
editor.reply.hint.pace.linger: Stays in the moment with detailed reactions; no time skips or big new events.
editor.reply.hint.pace.natural: How far the story moves depends on the player’s replies and what follows from them.
editor.reply.hint.perspective.card: Follows how the card is written.
editor.reply.hint.perspective.first_user: “I” is the player’s character, narrating what they see, hear, and feel in person.
editor.reply.hint.perspective.second_use: Narrates the player’s character as “you”, without acting for the player.
editor.reply.hint.perspective.third_limi: Third person, limited to what the point-of-view character knows.
editor.reply.hint.perspective.third_omni: The camera can cut to places the player’s character is not, showing what others do and think in private; the player’s character only knows what they have seen themselves.
editor.reply.hint.style.card: Follow character adds no writing guide of its own, so a card without style rules leaves the model to decide how to write.
editor.reply.hint.style.custom: Follows the style described here and changes only the prose, not the character or the layout.
editor.reply.hint.style.default: Default lets dialogue carry the scene with distinct character voices and narration kept to the essentials, and the card’s own style rules still come first.
editor.reply.hint.style.guided: Light guide keeps only the bones of the style and lets each model write in its own voice, so switching models changes the feel.
editor.reply.lede: Sets how this card replies by default. Anything a player has adjusted follows the player’s choice.
editor.reply.legacy.warn: These preferences include a value that is no longer supported, so players don’t get them right now. Choose a current option or reset everything to not set.

editor.reply.note.example.pace: e.g. A single scene can run for several turns

review.reasons.opening.no_reply_hook.sum: By the end of the opening, the player doesn't know what to say.
review.reasons.opening.no_reply_hook.fix: End on something the player can answer directly: a question, a few choices, or something that needs an immediate response. Choices are the most direct; see “Three ways to offer choices”.
review.reasons.opening.no_reply_hook.exa: The clerk slides a key across the counter: “Which room? Ground floor by the window, or the top floor?”
review.reasons.opening.no_reply_hook.opt: The “Opening choices” field in the editor. The player taps one and it fills the message box.
List a few numbered choices at the end of the opening, and the player replies with a number.
“1. Ground floor by the window  2. Top floor  3. See the rooms first”
Wrap the choices in [choices] and [/choices], one per line. They show as tappable buttons, and a tap fills the message box.

[choices]
Ground floor by the window
Top floor
[/choices]
review.reasons.opening.no_reply_hook.coa: Offering choices is the most direct hook, and any one of the three ways is enough. A question or an action at the end works too. Put it at the end of the opening.
review.reasons.opening.no_reply_hook.aft: You push open the tavern door. The owner looks up from the bar: “New face? Are you here to find someone, or to hide from someone?”
You push open the tavern door and the owner points at an empty seat: “New face?”  1. I'm looking for someone  2. I'm hiding  3. Just a drink
The opening is mood or general setting, with nothing happening right now.
Pick one concrete event and let it already be underway, so the player knows at once what they're facing.
Instead of “The city is quiet at night,” write “An alarm rings behind you, and the person at the door is staring at you.”
Decide that this scene has one event, then write it as already underway when the player arrives. One or two lines of atmosphere is enough.
This is an ancient city wrapped in fog, and its people each keep their own worries.
A bell tolls through the fog. The guard stops you: “The gates are shut, unless you have a pass.”
review.reasons.opening.exposition_only.s: The whole opening explains the world or a character, and the player isn't in a scene yet.
review.reasons.opening.exposition_only.f: Put the player in a scene and give the background they need through what characters do and say. Leave the rest to the character setup and Lorebook.
review.reasons.opening.exposition_only.e: Instead of “The world is split into three kingdoms,” write “The station announcer calls your name and asks if you'll board.”
review.reasons.opening.exposition_only.c: Split the background in two. What the player must know at once comes through a character's words or actions. The rest goes into the character setup and Lorebook, where it's used when the conversation needs it.
review.reasons.opening.exposition_only.b: The world is divided into three kingdoms that have fought for a hundred years, and magic is slowly fading in the war…
review.reasons.opening.exposition_only.a: The station announcer calls your name: “Please go to platform three. The train is about to leave.” Will you board?

review.reasons.opening.too_short.example: Turn “You came.” into “You came.” She pushes a freshly brewed cup across the table. “Sit. I have something to ask you.”
review.reasons.opening.too_short.coachFi: Add three things: who this is, where they are, and what's happening in front of the player. Then leave one action the player can respond to.
review.reasons.opening.too_short.after: “You came.” She pushes a freshly brewed cup to the edge of the table. Rain is still falling outside. “Sit. I have something to ask you.”

review.reasons.opening.unedited_generate: The opening stacks vague descriptions and stock phrases with repetitive sentence patterns, without the character's own voice.
Cut the generic mood filler and repeated dashes or ellipses, rewrite in the way this character actually talks, and end on a concrete event or choices.
Instead of “The gears of fate quietly began to turn as an unknown tension filled the air…,” write “She shoves a stack of flyers into your hands: ‘Don't just stand there. Help me hand these out.’”

Generated drafts often repeat the same paragraph structure and pile on vague adjectives and ellipses. Cut the stock atmosphere lines, replace them with what this character does and says, and end on a question or choices.
The night was dark as ink, and an almost imperceptible tension hung in the air… He stood quietly by the window, a complex emotion flashing across his deep eyes, as if waiting for fate to arrive.
He cracks the window open and waves you over: “There's a patrol downstairs. Are you taking the front door, or climbing the wall with me?”
review.reasons.character.copied_verbatim: The character setup pastes wiki articles, novel passages or another card's text verbatim instead of being written for conversation.
Summarize in your own words the character's background, their relationship to the player and how they talk. Characters from an existing work can be brief, but don't paste source text verbatim.
Instead of pasting “Former captain of Squad Two, retired after the war,” write “He's your former captain who now repairs boats at the harbor and speaks bluntly to people he knows.”

Wiki entries and novel excerpts are written for readers looking up a biography; pasting them straight in doesn't tell the character how to interact with the player. Keep only what matters for this conversation, and write in your own words who they are, how they relate to the player and how they talk. For characters from an existing work, those three things are enough.

Lin Mo, a major character in the series, first appears in Volume 1, Chapter 4. Born in the northern marches, he attended the academy in his youth before leaving to open an apothecary shop on the frontier. He is aloof in personality but skilled in medicine.

He runs a small apothecary shop on the frontier, and you're the apprentice who helps out at the counter. He speaks in short sentences, sticks to the point, and sighs before taking over whenever you mix up the herbs.

quality.retention.label: Kept playing
quality.retention.explain: The share of qualified players who started a chat and played {n} or more turns.
quality.retention.rules: Qualified players leave out the author, count several accounts on one device as one person, and must have played another author’s card; regenerated replies do not count as turns.
quality.lengthNote: Card length adds up the settings, lorebook entries and opening messages in use; opening pages and styling are not counted, and repeated text counts once. Counts are rounded, so the items may not add up exactly to the total.
